381.quote_or_event: “As a universal monarch with his fourfold army and great power, the possessor of the fourteen attributes of a king, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk.”
381.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana uses the cakravartin (universal monarch), with his fourfold army and fourteen royal treasures, as a byword for unmatched sovereign strength. A few verses earlier (11.20) it uses the other image found in this kural: the proud lion that is 'superior to all animals'.
381.tie_back: Valluvar's king with all six limbs of state stands among rulers like a lion among beasts. The Jain text draws on the same picture of the fully equipped monarch who has no equal, though it uses it to praise the learned monk.
381._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The royal imagery (army, power, insignia of kingship, the lion) matches closely, but the verse is a simile praising the learned monk, not a teaching on statecraft, so the fit is partial.

382.quote_or_event: “He (bears everything) like the earth; he annihilates (his Karman); he is free from greed; he, the Omniscient, does not keep store (of anything); he has crossed the ocean of life like the sea: he, the Hero, who grants protection to all, and whose perception is infinite.”
382.explanation: In the hymn to Mahavira, the ideal person is called the Hero (Vira), who gives protection, the gift of fearlessness (abhaya), to all beings, and whose knowledge has no limit. The same lecture ranks 'giving safety' as the best of gifts.
382.tie_back: Valluvar's four royal qualities are fearlessness, liberality, wisdom and energy. The Jain praise of Mahavira joins heroism, the giving of protection and boundless wisdom in a single figure, though it describes a spiritual hero rather than a king.
382.source: Sutrakritanga I.6.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; wisdomlib.org)
382._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Jacobi). Three of the kural's four qualities (courage, giving, wisdom) appear, but they describe the renunciant Mahavira, not a ruler, and Jain 'giving' here means protecting life rather than royal largesse.

383.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
383.explanation: Mahavira's sermon to his chief disciple Gautama repeats 'be careful all the while' (do not be heedless, pramada, even for a moment) as a refrain for all thirty-six verses. Sloth and delay are the danger he warns against most.
383.tie_back: Valluvar's first requirement is thoongaamai, a wakefulness that never puts off what must be done. Mahavira's refrain is the Jain version of the same never-sleeping vigilance, though he aims it at the soul's liberation rather than at governing a land.
383._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong match on unceasing alertness. However, the context is a monk's spiritual vigilance, and the kural's other two qualities (learning and resolve) are not addressed here.

384.quote_or_event: Indra: “Punishing thieves and robbers, cut-purses and burglars, you should establish public safety; thus you will be a Kshattriya.” Nami: “Men frequently apply punishment wrongly: the innocent are put in prison, and the perpetrator of the crime is set at liberty.”
384.explanation: Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, tests the renouncing king Nami by pressing royal duties on him, including rooting out wrongdoers. Nami answers that outward justice often misfires, and turns instead to conquering the passions within.
384.tie_back: Valluvar praises the king who never slips from dharma and removes what is unrighteous from the land. The Jain dialogue accepts that this is the warrior's duty but questions how reliable punishment is, and puts the deeper removal of wrong inside the self.
384._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The subject (a king's duty to put down wrong) is the same, but the Jain passage questions royal punishment rather than endorsing it, so this is a next-best contrast.

385.quote_or_event: “If there were numberless mountains of gold and silver, as big as Kailâsa, they would not satisfy a greedy man; for his avidity is boundless like space.”
385.explanation: When Indra tells King Nami to multiply his gold, jewels and treasury 'then you will be a true Kshattriya', Nami answers that no amount of wealth can satisfy craving. For laypeople, Jainism directs wealth through the vow of limiting possessions (parigraha-parimana) rather than through endless accumulation.
385.tie_back: Valluvar sets out how a government should create, collect, guard and distribute wealth. The Jain text, taking the renunciant's view, warns about the greed that a full treasury can feed, which is a counterweight to this kural, not a parallel.
385._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Jain scripture has no positive theory of royal public finance comparable to this kural. This is an honest contrast on the theme of the treasury, scored well below 60.

386.quote_or_event: “As giving safety is the best of gifts, as the best of true speeches is that which causes no distress, as chastity is the highest of austerities, so is the Śramaṇa Jñātṛputra the highest of men.”
386.explanation: In the hymn to Mahavira, the best speech is defined as true speech that causes no pain to others. This reflects the Jain vow of truthfulness, which is bound up with non-harm (ahimsa).
386.tie_back: Valluvar's beloved king is one who is not kadunjollan, a speaker of harsh words. The Jain ideal of truthful speech that causes no distress is the same standard of gentle speech, though the verse says nothing about how accessible a ruler is.
386.source: Sutrakritanga I.6.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; wisdomlib.org)
386._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Jacobi). It matches only the 'not harsh in speech' half of the kural. The ease of approaching the king has no direct Jain parallel here.

387.quote_or_event: Ishukara's queen Kamalavati to the king: “If the whole world and all treasures were yours, you would still not be satisfied, nor would all this be able to save you. Whenever you die, O king, and leave all pleasant things behind, the Law alone, and nothing else in this world, will save you, O monarch.”
387.explanation: The queen addresses the king gently, as 'O king' and 'O monarch', and points him to the Law (dharma) as the only real protection. In the story the whole court, king included, takes up the Jain path and reaches perfection.
387.tie_back: Valluvar says the world comes round to the ruler who joins kind words with giving and protection. In the Jain story it is the king who receives that kind of benevolent counsel, and the 'protection' it values is dharma rather than royal patronage.
387._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is a weak, next-best fit. Jain scripture offers no close parallel to winning the world's consent through sweet words, gifts and protection, and the passage reverses the kural's roles.

388.quote_or_event: “Here (on earth) you are the highest man, Reverend sir, and hereafter you will be the highest; exempt from all blemishes you will reach Perfection, a higher state than which there is none in this world.”
388.explanation: Sakra, king of the gods, throws off his disguise and worships King Nami, who has renounced his throne and mastered his passions. In Jainism even the gods bow to the perfected soul, and no ruler is divine by office.
388.tie_back: Valluvar says the just protector-king will be held by his people as a god. Jainism also ranks a royal figure above the gods, but only Nami, who has conquered himself, earns that honour, and a reigning king does not.
388._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Jainism is non-theistic and has no 'king as god' idea, so this is a next-best parallel on a king who is revered above gods because of virtue.

389.quote_or_event: “A man who returns, as it were, to the vomit, is not praised; but you want to confiscate the property left by the Brâhmaṇa.”
389.explanation: Queen Kamalavati sharply rebukes King Ishukara for planning to seize an heirless Brahmin's estate. The king takes this bitter criticism to heart: he renounces his kingdom, and the narrator reports that 'the king and the queen … they all reached perfection.'
389.tie_back: Valluvar promises that the world will shelter under the umbrella of the king who can bear words bitter to the ear. Ishukara is a Jain example of such a king, who accepts a stinging reproof and is raised by it.
389._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The story fits a king accepting a harsh rebuke well, but its outcome is renunciation, not better governance.

390.quote_or_event: Jain tradition remembers Rishabhanatha, the first Tirthankara, as the first king. Before he renounced, he ruled from Vinita (Ayodhya) and taught his people six means of livelihood: asi (arms for protection), masi (writing), krishi (agriculture), vidya (knowledge), vanijya (trade) and shilpa (crafts).
390.explanation: In the Jain account, the ideal first ruler protects his people and also equips them to live: he gives them arts, livelihoods and order. Only after that does he give up the throne for the ascetic path.
390.tie_back: Valluvar's 'light among kings' has generosity, compassion, a just sceptre and care for his people. Rishabha as first king is the Jain picture of exactly this kind of nurturing, protecting ruler.
390.source: Jain tradition on Rishabhanatha (Adipurana and Svetambara accounts), as summarised in Wikipedia, 'Rishabhanatha'
390._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from Wikipedia as a last resort, because primary-text pages (Trishashti, Kalpa Sutra on wisdomlib) were unavailable this session. The fit with a caring, protective ruler is good, but the four specific virtues are not named one by one.
